approved_text: Are there infinitely many natural numbers n such that, in the prime factorisation of n(n+1), distinct primes always appear with distinct exponents? That is, no two different prime factors of n(n+1) have the same exponent.
draft: Are there infinitely many natural numbers n such that, in the prime factorisation of n(n+1), distinct primes always appear with distinct exponents? That is, no two different prime factors of n(n+1) have the same exponent.
source_docstrings:
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that if
$$
  n(n + 1) = \prod_i p_i^{k_i}
$$
is the factorisation into distinct primes then all exponents $k_i$ are distinct?
